metadata.note: Framing facts for the two scoping slides. Every figure carries its date, its population, its printable source and its counterpoint. Citation keys point at the upstream corpus where one exists; the bibliography itself is never copied here.

source_kinds.primary: the study itself was opened and read
source_kinds.reported-in: the finding is reported by the cited source, whose own primary reference was not opened

claim.en: of students use generative AI to help with assessed work

population.en: 1,054 full-time UK undergraduates, polled by Savanta in December 2025; weighted for gender, institution type and year of study; margin of error approximately 3 %

freshness.en: Six months before this event. The third annual edition of the same instrument, so the trend is measured, not assembled.

trend.en: 89 % one year earlier, 53 % two years earlier

counterpoint.en: Using it is not the same as handing it in. Only 12 % include AI-generated text directly in assessed work; the dominant uses are having concepts explained (61 %) and articles summarised (49 %).

short.en: but only 12 % hand in AI-written text

caveat.en: UK undergraduates. No equivalent survey exists for Luxembourg.

source.reference: Rose Stephenson and Charlotte Armstrong, Student Generative AI Survey 2026, HEPI Report 199, Higher Education Policy Institute, 12 March 2026.

claim.en: time on the task, and 18 % higher output quality, with generative AI

population.en: 453 college-educated professionals in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial on occupation-specific writing tasks; half given ChatGPT

freshness.en: Three years old, and kept deliberately: it remains the peer-reviewed anchor in Science for generative-AI productivity in knowledge work, and no larger randomised replication has displaced it.

trend.en: The gain was largest for the weakest writers, compressing the spread between workers

counterpoint.en: The gain belongs to the task, not to the person. School students given an unguarded GPT-4 tutor scored 48 % higher while it was available and 17 % lower than the control group once it was taken away — a loss that disappeared when the tutor was constrained to give hints instead of answers.

source.reference: Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu, Haosen Ge, Özge Kabakcı and Rei Mariman, ‘Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics’, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26), e2422633122, 25 June 2025, doi:10.1073/pnas.2422633122.

population.en: nearly 1,000 high-school mathematics students in Turkey, field experiment

short.en: and 17 % lower once it is taken away

caveat.en: The two studies answer different questions — professionals performing, students learning — and that is the point: performing well and learning are not the same measurement.

source.reference: Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang, ‘Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence’, Science 381(6654), 187–192, 14 July 2023, doi:10.1126/science.adh2586.

claim.en: of essays by non-native English writers were wrongly flagged as AI-written — the average false-positive rate across seven detectors

population.en: 91 human-written TOEFL essays by non-native English writers, against 88 essays by US eighth-graders which the same detectors classified almost perfectly

freshness.en: Three years old and still load-bearing: the peer-reviewed position in 2026 is unchanged (Giray, Roe and Diesta Espiritu, ‘AI writing detectors are ineffective, unreliable and harmful’, English Teaching: Practice & Critique, 2026, doi:10.1108/ETPC-07-2025-0155). Detection is a fast-moving field — re-check before citing this in any policy document.

trend.en: 42 % of students say fear of being accused of cheating makes them less likely to use AI at all, down from 53 % a year earlier (HEPI 2026)

counterpoint.en: The vendors dispute it. Turnitin reports a document-level false-positive rate below 1 % and its own study finds no statistically significant bias against English-language learners; the newest detectors claim to have closed the gap.

source.reference: Turnitin, AI writing detection capabilities — frequently asked questions, Turnitin Knowledge Base.
source.verified: 2026-08-02, via Turnitin's current published claims; the FAQ page itself blocks automated retrieval

caveat.en: The authors call it a pilot on small samples, and most detectors tested were built on GPT-2. Turnitin's own detector was not among the seven. What the study establishes is the mechanism: detectors read plain vocabulary as machine-like — rewriting the same essays in richer English dropped the false-positive rate to 12 %. That mechanism is the one that matters in a multilingual university.

source.reference: Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yining Mao, Eric Wu and James Zou, ‘GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers’, Patterns 4(7), 100779, 2023, doi:10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779.

claim.en: of students say AI skills are essential to thrive — but only 48 % feel their teaching staff help them build those skills

population.en: 1,054 full-time UK undergraduates, polled by Savanta in December 2025; weighted; margin of error approximately 3 %

trend.en: Institutions are moving: 38 % now provide AI tools to their students, against 9 % two years earlier

counterpoint.en: The demand is not unanimous either. Half of students think their institution should provide AI tools — which means half do not — and a quarter disagree outright.

short.en: yet only half want it provided

caveat.en: Self-reported perception, not an audit of what is actually provided. The gap is widest in Arts and Humanities, where 26 % feel supported against 53 % in STEM.

source.reference: Rose Stephenson and Charlotte Armstrong, Student Generative AI Survey 2026, HEPI Report 199, Higher Education Policy Institute, 12 March 2026.

statement.en: None of this started in 2022. The benchmark against which every AI tutor is still measured — that one-to-one tutoring lifts students two standard deviations above classroom teaching — was published in 1984. Systematic reviews of AI in higher education were being written years before ChatGPT existed.

counterpoint.en: What broke in 2022 was not the idea. It was the scale: a research field became something every student has in their pocket.

note.en: Rendered as a sourced statement rather than a figure: a publication year has no population, and a figure without a population is an impression.

sources.reference: Benjamin S. Bloom, ‘The 2 sigma problem: the search for methods of group instruction as effective as one-to-one tutoring’, Educational Researcher 13(6), 4–16, 1984, doi:10.3102/0013189X013006004.

Olaf Zawacki-Richter, Victoria I. Marín, Melissa Bond and Franziska Gouverneur, ‘Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education — where are the educators?’, International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 16, 39, 2019, doi:10.1186/s41239-019-0171-0.

Thomas K. F. Chiu, Qi Xia, Xinyan Zhou, Ching-Sing Chai and Miaoting Cheng, ‘Systematic literature review on opportunities, challenges, and future research recommendations of artificial intelligence in education’, Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 4, 100118, 2023, doi:10.1016/j.caeai.2022.100118.

examples.en: Introductory programming stopped being a filter. In 2022 OpenAI Codex already scored above the median student on a CS1 final exam; a year later it still beat median students on second-year data-structure exercises, though the margin narrowed on problems requiring novel design.

source.reference: James Finnie-Ansley, Paul Denny, Brett A. Becker, Andrew Luxton-Reilly and James Prather, ‘The robots are coming: exploring the implications of OpenAI Codex on introductory programming’, ACE 2022, ACM, 10–19, doi:10.1145/3511861.3511863; and Finnie-Ansley et al., ‘My AI wants to know if this will be on the exam: testing OpenAI’s Codex on CS2 programming exercises’, ACE 2023, ACM, 97–104, doi:10.1145/3576123.3576134.

caveat.en: Measured on exams as they were written at the time. The result is as much about assessment design as about the model.

examples.en: In medicine the danger is confidence, not error. Medical students working virtual patient cases with AI support and no human feedback produced the least accurate diagnoses of the whole cohort — and were the most confident of any group.

source.reference: Reported as case study one in Stephenson and Armstrong, Student Generative AI Survey 2026, HEPI Report 199, 12 March 2026; study by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, Erasmus University Rotterdam, the University of Campinas and McMaster University, using the Isabel Clinical Educator.

caveat.en: Reported inside the HEPI survey; the underlying study was not opened. Cite the primary paper before using this in any policy setting.

headline.en: AI alone: least accurate, most confident

examples.en: Purpose-built legal research tools — sold to lawyers, marketed as hallucination-free — still invent law: on more than 200 open-ended legal queries, 17 % of Lexis+ AI answers and 33 % of Westlaw AI-Assisted Research answers were hallucinated.

source.reference: Varun Magesh, Faiz Surani, Matthew Dahl, Mirac Suzgun, Christopher D. Manning and Daniel E. Ho, ‘Hallucination-free? Assessing the reliability of leading AI legal research tools’, Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, 2025, doi:10.1111/jels.12413.

caveat.en: Paywalled; figures taken from the authors’ open preprint and consistent secondary reporting. The vendors have updated their systems since the queries were run.

headline.en: Legal AI tools still invent case law

examples.en: General-purpose models are far worse, and do not know it: asked specific, verifiable questions about randomly chosen US federal court cases, they hallucinated between 58 % of the time (GPT-4) and 88 % (Llama 2), and often accepted a false legal premise handed to them in the question.

source.reference: Matthew Dahl, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun and Daniel E. Ho, ‘Large legal fictions: profiling legal hallucinations in large language models’, Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1), 64–93, 2024, doi:10.1093/jla/laae003.

caveat.en: US case law. The failure mode — fluent, confident and wrong — transfers to any jurisdiction; the rates do not.

headline.en: General models wrong most of the time

examples.en: The edge is jagged, not general. Given eighteen realistic consulting tasks, 758 consultants using GPT-4 produced better and faster work on tasks inside the model’s competence — and worse work than the control group on tasks just outside it, because plausible wrong answers were accepted uncritically.

source.reference: Fabrizio Dell’Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick et al., ‘Navigating the jagged technological frontier: field experimental evidence of the effects of AI on knowledge worker productivity and quality’, Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013, 2023.

caveat.en: A working paper, run inside one consulting firm, and co-authored with that firm. The concept it introduced — the jagged frontier — has outlived the specific numbers.

headline.en: Better inside the frontier, worse just outside

examples.en: Writing in a second language is read as writing by a machine. Seven detectors wrongly flagged 61 % of essays by non-native English writers while classifying US eighth-grade essays almost perfectly — and rewriting the very same essays in richer vocabulary dropped the rate to 12 %. In a university where most students write in a language that is not their first, this is not an abstract concern.

source.reference: Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yining Mao, Eric Wu and James Zou, ‘GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers’, Patterns 4(7), 100779, 2023, doi:10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779.

caveat.en: Pilot study, small samples, detectors mostly built on GPT-2. The mechanism it identifies — plain vocabulary read as machine-like — is what carries.

headline.en: Detectors read a second language as machine

examples.en: Access can raise the score and lower the learning. Nearly a thousand school students gained 48 % on practice problems with an unguarded GPT-4 tutor and then scored 17 % below the control group on the exam they sat without it. Constraining the same tutor to hints instead of answers removed the loss.

source.reference: Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu, Haosen Ge, Özge Kabakcı and Rei Mariman, ‘Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics’, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26), e2422633122, 2025, doi:10.1073/pnas.2422633122.

caveat.en: School mathematics in Turkey, over weeks. Whether it holds over a degree, nobody has measured yet.

examples.en: Arts and humanities students are the most sceptical and the least supported: 25 % think AI-written work would earn a good grade in their subject, against 46 % in STEM — and only 26 % feel their teaching staff help them build AI skills, against 53 % in STEM.

source.reference: Rose Stephenson and Charlotte Armstrong, Student Generative AI Survey 2026, HEPI Report 199, Higher Education Policy Institute, 12 March 2026.

caveat.en: UK subject areas, which do not map cleanly onto this university’s three faculties. Read as a disciplinary gradient, not as a faculty measurement.

no_faculty_data.en: No survey measures generative-AI adoption faculty by faculty at the University of Luxembourg. Every figure here comes from studies run elsewhere — mostly the United Kingdom and the United States — and describes a discipline, not this institution. Read them as what your field is already living through, not as a measurement of this room.

headline.en: Nobody has measured this at our University.
